children.title: Epigraphical Representations
children.top_down_role: Set representations connecting functions, levels, and lifted constraints.

children.title: Epigraph-Hypograph Representation Pair
children.top_down_role: Upper and lower set representations of extended-real functions.

children.title: Epigraph Geometry
children.top_down_role: Local geometry of upper-set representations of extended-real functions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}f\) uniquely determines \(f\) through its vertical sections.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic epigraph representation for an extended-real-valued function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}f:=\{(x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R:f(x)\le r\},\qquad (\operatorname{epi}f)_x=\{r\in\mathbb R:f(x)\le r\}.\] Each section is respectively \(\varnothing\), \(\mathbb R\), or an upper ray when \(f(x)=+\infty\), \(f(x)=-\infty\), or \(f(x)\in\mathbb R\). With \(\inf\varnothing:=+\infty\), the recovery formula is \[f(x)=\inf (\operatorname{epi}f)_x.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph consists of all points lying vertically above the function and recovers every function value as the infimum of the corresponding vertical section.
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Geometry

children.title: Hypograph Geometry
children.top_down_role: Local geometry of lower-set representations of extended-real functions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{hypo}g\) uniquely determines \(g\) through its vertical sections.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic hypograph representation for an extended-real-valued function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\operatorname{hypo}g:=\{(x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R:r\le g(x)\},\qquad (\operatorname{hypo}g)_x=\{r\in\mathbb R:r\le g(x)\}.\] Each section is respectively \(\varnothing\), \(\mathbb R\), or a lower ray when \(g(x)=-\infty\), \(g(x)=+\infty\), or \(g(x)\in\mathbb R\). With \(\sup\varnothing:=-\infty\), the recovery formula is \[g(x)=\sup (\operatorname{hypo}g)_x.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hypograph consists of all points lying vertically below the function and recovers every function value as the supremum of the corresponding vertical section.
knowledge_statements.title: Hypograph Geometry

children.title: Sign-Reversal Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural passage between epigraphical and hypographical viewpoints.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonempty set and \(g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reflection of \(\operatorname{hypo}g\) in the height coordinate equals \(\operatorname{epi}(-g)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact epigraph–hypograph correspondence under sign reversal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \((x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R\), \[(x,r)\in\operatorname{hypo}g\iff r\le g(x)\iff -r\ge -g(x)\iff (x,-r)\in\operatorname{epi}(-g).\] Consequently, \[R(\operatorname{hypo}g)=\operatorname{epi}(-g),\qquad R(\operatorname{epi}g)=\operatorname{hypo}(-g).\] When \(X\) is topological, this reflection also interchanges upper semicontinuity of \(g\) with lower semicontinuity of \(-g\); on a vector space it interchanges concavity of \(g\) with convexity of \(-g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negating function values and reflecting the vertical coordinate converts hypographs into epigraphs, upper semicontinuity into lower semicontinuity, and concavity into convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Reversal Correspondence

children.title: One-Sided Representation Asymmetry
children.top_down_role: Differences in upper-facing and lower-facing local geometric behavior.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Epigraph and hypograph geometry encode opposite one-sided regularity and curvature properties of the same function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymmetry between lower and upper geometric encodings of one function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lower representation satisfies \[\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is closed}\iff f\text{ is lower semicontinuous},\qquad \operatorname{epi}f\text{ is convex}\iff f\text{ is convex}.\] The upper representation satisfies \[\operatorname{hypo}f\text{ is closed}\iff f\text{ is upper semicontinuous},\qquad \operatorname{hypo}f\text{ is convex}\iff f\text{ is concave}.\] Thus a single orientation does not encode both lower and upper regularity or both convexity and concavity; the opposite information is obtained by sign reversal and vertical reflection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epigraphs encode lower semicontinuity and convexity, whereas hypographs encode upper semicontinuity and concavity; one orientation generally cannot replace the other.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Representation Asymmetry

children.title: Level-Set Representation Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Geometric organization through active levels and sublevel systems.

children.title: Level-Set Geometry
children.top_down_role: Local geometry restricted to a fixed function level.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a set, \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact level is the intersection of the corresponding sublevel and superlevel sets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact level sets as two-sided threshold geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[L_{=\alpha}(f):=\{x\in X:f(x)=\alpha\},\quad L_{\le\alpha}(f):=\{x\in X:f(x)\le\alpha\},\quad L_{\ge\alpha}(f):=\{x\in X:f(x)\ge\alpha\}.\] Then \[L_{=\alpha}(f)=L_{\le\alpha}(f)\cap L_{\ge\alpha}(f)=L_{\le\alpha}(f)\setminus\{x\in X:f(x)<\alpha\}.\] Unlike the family of sublevel sets, distinct exact levels are disjoint rather than nested.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact level set contains points attaining one threshold. It is the intersection of the matching sublevel and superlevel sets, and distinct exact levels are disjoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Level-Set Geometry

children.title: Sublevel-Set Geometry
children.top_down_role: Local geometry of threshold-bounded function regions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a set, \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sublevel sets are horizontal epigraph slices projected onto \(X\), and they are nested by threshold.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sublevel sets as nested horizontal slices of an epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sublevel set at height \(\alpha\) is \[L_\alpha(f):=\{x\in X:f(x)\le\alpha\}=\{x\in X:(x,\alpha)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}.\] Equivalently, \[L_\alpha(f)\times\{\alpha\}=\operatorname{epi}f\cap(X\times\{\alpha\}).\] If \(\alpha\le\beta\), then \[L_\alpha(f)\subseteq L_\beta(f).\] Moreover, the nested family determines the function through \[f(x)=\inf\{\alpha\in\mathbb R:x\in L_\alpha(f)\},\] with \(\inf\varnothing:=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sublevel sets are horizontal slices of the epigraph. They expand monotonically with the threshold and, taken over all thresholds, determine the function.
knowledge_statements.title: Sublevel-Set Geometry

children.title: Active-Level Localization
children.top_down_role: Connections between boundary points of sublevel systems and their active levels.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a set, \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Activity at level \(\alpha\) is localized by removing the strict sublevel from the nonstrict sublevel.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Localization of points where a threshold inequality is active.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[A_\alpha(f):=\{x\in X:f(x)=\alpha\},\qquad L_{<\alpha}(f):=\{x\in X:f(x)<\alpha\}.\] Then, globally and after restriction to any set \(U\), \[A_\alpha(f)=L_\alpha(f)\setminus L_{<\alpha}(f),\qquad A_\alpha(f)\cap U=(L_\alpha(f)\cap U)\setminus(L_{<\alpha}(f)\cap U).\] At an active point \(\bar x\), the epigraph point \((\bar x,\alpha)\) is the least-height point of the vertical fiber \(\{r:(\bar x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A threshold is active exactly where the function equals it. Locally, active points are obtained by subtracting the strict sublevel set from the nonstrict sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Level Localization

children.title: Threshold-Perturbation Geometry
children.top_down_role: Changes in level-based geometry as the reference threshold varies.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a set, \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and \(\alpha,t\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Perturbing a threshold is equivalent to applying the opposite constant perturbation to the function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact identities for additive perturbations of level thresholds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an additive threshold perturbation \(t\), \[L_{\alpha+t}(f)=\{x:f(x)\le\alpha+t\}=L_\alpha(f-t),\qquad L_\alpha(f+t)=L_{\alpha-t}(f).\] The associated epigraphs obey the vertical-translation identity \[\operatorname{epi}(f+t)=\{(x,r+t):(x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}.\] Hence increasing the threshold expands the feasible sublevel family, while increasing the function by the same amount contracts it by the corresponding threshold shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Raising a sublevel threshold by a constant is equivalent to lowering the function by that constant; epigraphs undergo the corresponding vertical translation.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold-Perturbation Geometry

children.title: Indicator-Set Geometry Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Translation between closed-set geometry and extended-real function geometry.

children.title: Indicator-Function Embeddings
children.top_down_role: Encoding closed-set geometry within extended-real function representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator-Function Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real indicator embedding of a set and its constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\delta_C(x):=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\] Then \[\operatorname{dom}\delta_C=C,\qquad \operatorname{epi}\delta_C=C\times[0,+\infty),\qquad \{x\in X:\delta_C(x)\le\alpha\}=\begin{cases}\varnothing,&\alpha<0,\\C,&\alpha\ge0.\end{cases}\] For every \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), constrained minimization is equivalently encoded by \[\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(f(x)+\delta_C(x)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator function assigns zero on a set and positive infinity outside it, thereby encoding membership, epigraph geometry, sublevel geometry, and constrained minimization for functions that do not take negative infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The extended-real indicator embeds membership in \(C\) as finite-valuedness, embeds \(C\) into epigraph geometry, and encodes constrained minimization for functions valued in \(\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\).

children.title: Closed-Set Embeddings
children.top_down_role: Placement of set geometry into broader epigraphical constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Set Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological closed-set embedding through extended-real indicators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the indicator \(\delta_C:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), the following conditions are equivalent: \[C\text{ is closed};\qquad \delta_C\text{ is lower semicontinuous};\qquad \operatorname{epi}\delta_C=C\times[0,+\infty)\text{ is closed in }X\times\mathbb R.\] Every finite sublevel set of \(\delta_C\) is either \(\varnothing\) or \(C\). If \(X\) is also a real vector space, then \[C\text{ is convex}\iff\delta_C\text{ is convex}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is closed exactly when its indicator is lower semicontinuous, equivalently when the indicator epigraph is closed. In a real vector space, convex sets likewise correspond to convex indicators.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space and \(C\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Closed subsets of \(X\) correspond exactly to lower-semicontinuous indicator functions and closed indicator epigraphs; when \(X\) is a real vector space, convex subsets correspond exactly to convex indicators.

children.title: Normal–Subdifferential Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Navigation between set normals and generalized derivative geometry of indicator functions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real locally convex space with continuous dual \(X^*\).
\(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The convex subdifferential of \(\delta_C\) equals the convex-analytic normal cone to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-analytic normal cone as an indicator subdifferential.

source_refs.locator: 2.5.2 Specific Normal and Subdifferential Structures p. 235
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in C\), define \[N_C(x):=\{x^*\in X^*:\langle x^*,y-x\rangle\le0\ \text{for every }y\in C\}.\] With both sides defined as \(\varnothing\) for \(x\notin C\), one has \[\partial\delta_C(x)=N_C(x).\] Thus the subgradient inequality for the indicator, \[\delta_C(y)\ge\delta_C(x)+\langle x^*,y-x\rangle\quad\text{for every }y\in X,\] is exactly the normal-cone inequality on feasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex set, the subdifferential of its indicator function is exactly its convex normal cone, with both objects empty outside the set.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal–Subdifferential Correspondence

source_witnesses.locator: 2.5.2 Specific Normal and Subdifferential Structures p. 235
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Domain-Boundary Encoding
children.top_down_role: Representation of feasible-set boundaries through extended-real domains.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space and \(C\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The domain of \(\delta_C\) recovers \(C\), and its topological boundary is recoverable entirely from finite-valuedness.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding a set and its topological boundary by an indicator domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \[\operatorname{dom}\delta_C:=\{x\in X:\delta_C(x)<+\infty\}=C,\] the indicator records the set boundary as \[\partial_{\mathrm{top}}C=\overline{\operatorname{dom}\delta_C}\setminus\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\delta_C).\] Equivalently, \(x\in\partial_{\mathrm{top}}C\) precisely when every neighborhood of \(x\) contains a point where \(\delta_C\) is finite and a point where \(\delta_C=+\infty\). Thus finite-valuedness versus infinite-valuedness encodes both the domain and its boundary interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indicator's finite-valued domain is the encoded set. Boundary points are exactly those whose every neighborhood meets both the finite and infinite regions.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Boundary Encoding

children.title: Epigraphical Tangent Geometry
children.top_down_role: Tangent structures of epigraphs and their level-set projections.

children.title: Epigraphical Tangent Cones
children.top_down_role: First-order tangent geometry of epigraphs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,\bar r)=\operatorname{epi}df(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Contingent tangent cone to a set at a point.
Lower subderivative of the extended-real-valued function.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional contingent tangent formula using the lower subderivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the lower subderivative by \[df(\bar x)(w):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\w'\to w}}\frac{f(\bar x+t w')-f(\bar x)}{t}.\] Then the contingent tangent cone to the epigraph satisfies \[T_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))=\{(w,\eta)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:df(\bar x)(w)\leq\eta\}=\operatorname{epi}df(\bar x).\] Thus first-order epigraphical directions are exactly the pairs whose vertical component dominates the directional first-order growth of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tangent cone to an epigraph is the epigraph of the function's lower subderivative at the base point.
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraphical Tangent Cones

children.title: Level-Set Tangent Geometry
children.top_down_role: Tangent relationships among epigraphs, sublevels, and active levels.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{w:df(\bar x)(w)<0\}\subset T_S(\bar x)\subset\{w:df(\bar x)(w)\leq0\}\).

notation.meaning: Active sublevel set at the reference value.
Lower subderivative at the reference point.
Contingent tangent cone to the sublevel set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General contingent inclusions; equality at zero requires additional regularity.

source_refs.locator: B. Level Sets and Intersections p. 42

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(df(\bar x)\) defined by the lower difference-quotient limit, the active sublevel has the tangent bounds \[\{w\in\mathbb{R}^n:df(\bar x)(w)<0\}\subset T_S(\bar x)\subset\{w\in\mathbb{R}^n:df(\bar x)(w)\leq0\}.\] The right inclusion follows from feasibility along tangent sequences, while strict negative first-order growth gives the left inclusion. Directions satisfying \(df(\bar x)(w)=0\) need not be tangent without an additional derivability or constraint-regularity hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strictly descending directions are tangent to the active sublevel, and every sublevel tangent direction has nonpositive lower subderivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Level-Set Tangent Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: B. Level Sets and Intersections p. 42

children.title: Vertical Epigraph Normals
children.top_down_role: Epigraphical normals associated with ordinary first-order function geometry.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(\bar x)=\{v:(v,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\}\).

notation.meaning: Limiting normal cone to a set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting-normal definition of ordinary subgradients through normalized nonhorizontal epigraph normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The limiting subdifferential of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) is the horizontal component of epigraph normals whose vertical component is normalized to \(-1\): \[\partial f(\bar x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:(v,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\}.\] More generally, every epigraph normal of the form \((v,-\lambda)\) with \(\lambda>0\) corresponds, by conicity, to the ordinary subgradient \(v/\lambda\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary limiting subgradients are precisely epigraph normals normalized to have vertical component minus one.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertical Epigraph Normals

children.title: Horizontal Epigraph Normals
children.top_down_role: Epigraphical normals associated with horizon and singular behavior.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{v:(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\}\).

notation.meaning: Limiting normal cone to a set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional limiting horizon subdifferential represented by horizontal epigraph normals.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.2 Representations of Singular Subgradients and Horizontal Normals to Graphs and Epigraphs p. 223
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The limiting horizon subdifferential of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) is defined by the horizontal epigraph normals \[\partial^\infty f(\bar x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\}.\] Unlike normals with a strictly negative vertical component, these normals cannot be rescaled to the ordinary normalization \(-1\). They record singular first-order behavior and can obstruct normal-cone calculus and local Lipschitz regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Horizon subgradients are exactly the horizontal limiting normals to the epigraph at the graph point.
knowledge_statements.title: Horizontal Epigraph Normals

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4.2 Representations of Singular Subgradients and Horizontal Normals to Graphs and Epigraphs p. 223
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Level-Set Normal Geometry
children.top_down_role: Normal relationships among epigraphs, sublevels, and active levels.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\{f\leq\alpha\}}(\bar x)=\{w:\langle\nabla f(\bar x),w\rangle\leq0\}\) and \(N_{\{f\leq\alpha\}}(\bar x)=\{\lambda\nabla f(\bar x):\lambda\geq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth nondegenerate active-level formula for tangent and normal geometry.

For the active sublevel \(S:=\{x:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) and active level \(L:=\{x:f(x)=\alpha\}\), nonvanishing of the gradient yields \[T_S( ar x)=\{w:\langle

children.title: Epigraphical Asymptotic Geometry
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic directions of epigraphs and their relation to growth and coercivity.

children.title: Epigraphical Horizon Cones
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic directions visible through unbounded epigraph sequences.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^\infty=\{(d,\tau):\exists\lambda_k\downarrow0,\ (x_k,r_k)\in C,\ \lambda_k(x_k,r_k)\to(d,\tau)\}\).

notation.meaning: Positive scaling sequence tending to zero.
A direction in the product space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential finite-dimensional definition of the horizon cone of an epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The horizon cone of the epigraph \(C:=\operatorname{epi}f\) is \[C^\infty:=\{(d,\tau)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:\exists\lambda_k\downarrow0,\ \exists(x_k,r_k)\in C,\ \lambda_k(x_k,r_k)\to(d,\tau)\}.\] Equivalently, its elements are finite limiting directions obtained by shrinking possibly unbounded epigraph points. The definition is independent of translating \(C\) by any fixed vector, because the scaled translation vanishes as \(\lambda_k\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraphical horizon cone consists of finite limits obtained by scaling unbounded epigraph points toward the origin.
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraphical Horizon Cones

children.title: Epigraphical Recession Geometry
children.top_down_role: Persistent large-scale directions of epigraphs.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\operatorname{epi}f)^\infty=\operatorname{epi}f^\infty\).

notation.meaning: Recession function of the convex function.
Recession cone of a closed convex set.
A reference point in the effective domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex epigraph formula for persistent recession directions.

source_refs.locator: D. Cones and Convex Sets p. 118

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the convex recession function by \[f^\infty(d):=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f}\bigl(f(x+d)-f(x)\bigr)=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{f(\bar x+t d)-f(\bar x)}{t}.\] Then the persistent directions of the epigraph satisfy \[(\operatorname{epi}f)^\infty=\{(d,\tau):f^\infty(d)\leq\tau\}=\operatorname{epi}f^\infty.\] Equivalently, \((d,\tau)\) belongs to this cone exactly when \((x,r)+t(d,\tau)\in\operatorname{epi}f\) for every \((x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f\) and every \(t\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed proper convex function, the recession cone of its epigraph is the epigraph of its recession function.
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraphical Recession Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: D. Cones and Convex Sets p. 118

children.title: Noncoercive Escape Geometry
children.top_down_role: Epigraphical mechanisms permitting minimizing sequences to escape.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is not level-bounded if and only if some sequence satisfies \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\) and \(\sup_k f(x_k)<\infty\).

notation.meaning: Escape direction obtained from normalized iterates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional characterization of escape through unbounded bounded-height sublevels.

source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is not level-bounded exactly when some sublevel \(L_\alpha:=\{x:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is unbounded, equivalently when there exists \((x_k)\) such that \[\|x_k\|\to\infty\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sup_k f(x_k)<\infty.\] After taking a subsequence, \(x_k/\|x_k\|\to d\) for some \(\|d\|=1\), and the epigraph points \((x_k,\alpha)\) show that \[(d,0)\in(\operatorname{epi}f)^\infty.\] Thus bounded-height escape produces a nonzero horizontal epigraphical horizon direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure of level boundedness is exactly escape to infinity with bounded objective values, producing a nonzero horizontal epigraph horizon direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Noncoercive Escape Geometry

source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

children.title: Epi-Regularity
children.top_down_role: Regularity classes expressed through local tangent, normal, and projection geometry of epigraphs.

children.title: Clarke-Regular Epigraphs
children.top_down_role: Epigraphs with coherent regular and limiting first-order geometry.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is Clarke regular at \(\bar z\) exactly when \(\widehat N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar z)=N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar z)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise Clarke regularity of the epigraph as a closed set.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The epigraph of \(f\) is Clarke regular at \(\bar z:=(\bar x,f(\bar x))\) when it is locally closed there and its Fréchet and limiting normal cones coincide: \[\widehat N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar z)=N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar z).\] Equivalently, every limiting epigraph normal at \(\bar z\) already satisfies the regular first-order support inequality at that same point. This definition applies simultaneously to normals with negative vertical component and to horizontal normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epigraph is Clarke regular when its regular and limiting normal cones agree at the graph point.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke-Regular Epigraphs

source_witnesses.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

children.title: Prox-Regular Epigraphs
children.top_down_role: Epigraphs retaining locally stable proximal geometry.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is locally prox-regular at \(\bar z\) when its nearby unit limiting normals satisfy a uniform quadratic support inequality.

notation.meaning: Limiting normal cone to the epigraph.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform local set-based prox-regularity of an epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The epigraph \(C:=\operatorname{epi}f\) is locally prox-regular at \(\bar z\) if there exist \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(r\geq0\) such that, whenever \(z,z'\in C\cap B_\varepsilon(\bar z)\) and \(v\in N_C(z)\) with \(\|v\|\leq1\), \[\langle v,z'-z\rangle\leq\frac r2\|z'-z\|^2.\] The same constants control all nearby epigraph points and unit limiting normals, expressing a uniform local lower bound on the radius of external supporting balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prox-regular epigraph has a uniform local quadratic support bound for every nearby unit limiting normal.
knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regular Epigraphs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated uniform quadratic normal inequality is a standard characterization under an appropriate set-level prox-regularity convention, but the cited locator is only the opening of the variational-geometry chapter and does not specifically identify prox-regularity. Because terminology, neighborhood quantifiers, and curvature/radius parameterization vary across sources, a specific definition or theorem locator is required before accepting this exact formulation.

children.title: Epi-Regularity Failures
children.top_down_role: Cusps, cliffs, horizon abnormalities, and incompatible epigraphical normal systems.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat N_C(\bar z)=\{0\}\) while \(N_C(\bar z)\) contains \(\mathbb{R}_+(-1,-1)\cup\mathbb{R}_+(1,-1)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete downward-cusp failure of epigraphical Clarke regularity.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x):=-|x|\), let \(C:=\operatorname{epi}f\). At the cusp \(\bar z:=(0,0)\), the regular normal cone is \[\widehat N_C(\bar z)=\{(0,0)\}.\] Normals along the two smooth boundary branches converge to nonzero normals at the cusp, giving \[\mathbb{R}_+(-1,-1)\cup\mathbb{R}_+(1,-1)\subset N_C(\bar z).\] Hence \(\widehat N_C(\bar z)\neq N_C(\bar z)\), so the epigraph is not Clarke regular and therefore cannot satisfy the uniform prox-regularity condition there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The downward cusp of minus absolute value has only the zero regular normal but has nonzero limiting branch normals.
knowledge_statements.title: Epi-Regularity Failures

source_witnesses.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

children.title: Clarke-Regular Sets

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is Clarke regular at \(\bar x\) exactly when \(\widehat N_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)\).

Clarke regularity on a subset means that this pointwise equality holds at every point of that subset.

children.title: Uniform Normal-Regularity Classes
children.top_down_role: Uniform regularity classes based on controlled local normal variation.

children.title: Super-Regular Set Geometry
children.top_down_role: Uniform local normal behavior associated with super-regular sets.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is super-regular at \(\bar x\) exactly when the stated uniform normal-angle estimate holds.

notation.meaning: Limiting normal cone to C at x.
Open ball of radius delta centered at x-bar.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local definition using limiting normals and a uniform two-point estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(C\) is super-regular at \(\bar x\) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
\langle v,z-x\rangle\leq \varepsilon\|v\|\,\|z-x\|
\]
for all \(x,z\in C\cap B_\delta(\bar x)\) and every \(v\in N_C(x)\). Thus normals based at any nearby point make, uniformly, at most an arbitrarily small positive angle defect with chords joining that point to any other nearby point of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Super-regularity requires every nearby normal to satisfy an arbitrarily accurate supporting-angle inequality against every nearby chord of the set.
knowledge_statements.title: Super-Regular Set Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically plausible and fits the leaf, but no inspectable citation supports the exact limiting-normal convention and quantifiers.

children.title: Subsmooth Set Geometry
children.top_down_role: Controlled local normal variation associated with subsmooth sets.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is subsmooth at \(\bar x\) exactly when its bounded Clarke-normal mapping is locally approximately monotone.

notation.meaning: Clarke normal cone to C at x.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local finite-dimensional definition through approximate monotonicity of bounded Clarke normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(C\) is subsmooth at \(\bar x\) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
\langle v_1-v_2,x_1-x_2\rangle\geq-\varepsilon\|x_1-x_2\|
\]
whenever \(x_1,x_2\in C\cap B_\delta(\bar x)\) and \(v_i\in N_C^C(x_i)\cap\mathbb B\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\). The normalization by \(\mathbb B\) makes the error uniform over bounded normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subsmoothness means that nearby bounded Clarke normals obey a uniform approximate-monotonicity inequality with arbitrarily small linear error.
knowledge_statements.title: Subsmooth Set Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The approximate-monotonicity definition fits the leaf, but its precise normalization and Clarke-normal convention require an authoritative source.

children.title: Regularity-Class Comparison
children.top_down_role: Relative strength, overlap, and geometric coverage of the two classes.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional and \(C\subset X\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\).
All regularity notions use their standard local finite-dimensional normal-cone conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{prox-regular}\Rightarrow\text{super-regular}\Longleftrightarrow\text{subsmooth}\Rightarrow\text{Clarke regular}\), while the reverse implications fail in general.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional comparison; infinite-dimensional equivalences may require additional compactness assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At \(\bar x\), local prox-regularity of \(C\) implies super-regularity. In finite dimensions, super-regularity is equivalent to subsmoothness, and either property implies Clarke regularity. Consequently,
\[
\text{prox-regular}\;\Longrightarrow\;\text{super-regular}\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\text{subsmooth}\;\Longrightarrow\;\text{Clarke regular}.
\]
Without additional hypotheses, neither Clarke regularity implies super-regularity nor super-regularity implies prox-regularity; hence the displayed one-way implications cannot generally be reversed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Locally, prox-regularity implies super-regularity; in finite dimensions super-regularity and subsmoothness coincide, and both imply Clarke regularity. The remaining converses fail generally.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularity-Class Comparison

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison property fits the container, but the equivalence and asserted failure of both converses need specific supporting results or examples.

children.title: Uniformity Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Local regimes where the relevant normal-control properties cease to be uniform.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\) in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A fixed-base Clarke-normal estimate does not entail a neighborhood-uniform two-point estimate.

notation.meaning: Regular and limiting normal cones, respectively.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifier boundary between pointwise Clarke regularity and neighborhood-uniform normal regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Clarke regularity at \(\bar x\), expressed by \(\widehat N_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)\), controls normals only at the fixed base point. Super-regularity instead requires that, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), one common neighborhood satisfy
\[
\langle v,z-x\rangle\leq\varepsilon\|v\|\,\|z-x\|
\]
simultaneously for all nearby \(x,z\in C\) and all \(v\in N_C(x)\). Losing this common neighborhood is precisely the uniformity failure; pointwise convergence of normal estimates does not restore it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clarke regularity fixes the normal base point, whereas super-regularity uses one neighborhood for all nearby bases and chords. The first quantifier pattern does not imply the second.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniformity Failure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quantifier distinction fits this failure-boundary leaf, but the claimed nonimplication requires a cited separating example or theorem.

children.title: Directional Set Regularity
children.top_down_role: Regularity localized to selected approach directions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional, \(C\subset X\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\), and \(D\subset\mathbb S_X\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed restricted estimate defines super-regularity along the selected approach directions \(D\).

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to D.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A directional super-regularity condition; the literature contains other directional localization conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(D\subset\mathbb S_X\), say that \(C\) is super-regular at \(\bar x\) along \(D\) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(\delta>0\) and \(\eta>0\) such that
\[
\langle v,z-x\rangle\leq\varepsilon\|v\|\,\|z-x\|
\]
for all \(x,z\in C\cap B_\delta(\bar x)\), \(v\in N_C(x)\), whose nonzero approach vectors satisfy \(d((x-\bar x)/\|x-\bar x\|,D)<\eta\) and \(d((z-\bar x)/\|z-\bar x\|,D)<\eta\). The corresponding restriction is omitted when an approach vector is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional super-regularity imposes the uniform normal-angle estimate only on nearby points approaching the reference point through selected directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Directional Set Regularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Directional regularity has several inequivalent localization conventions. No source establishes this particular two-point directional restriction as the intended canonical condition.

children.title: Prox-Regular Set Geometry
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex geometry retaining locally stable projection and proximal normals.

children.title: Local Prox-Regularity
children.top_down_role: Pointwise and localized proximal regularity.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is closed in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local prox-regularity is the existence of a neighborhood and a positive radius satisfying the quadratic proximal-normal inequality.

notation.meaning: Proximal normal cone to C at x.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Localized set-level prox-regularity, uniform over nearby unit proximal normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(C\) is locally prox-regular at \(\bar x\) if there exist \(r>0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
\langle v,z-x\rangle\leq\frac{1}{2r}\|z-x\|^2
\]
for every \(x,z\in C\cap B_\delta(\bar x)\) and every \(v\in N_C^P(x)\) with \(\|v\|=1\). Equivalently, sufficiently short outward proximal-normal displacements from nearby points have those points as their unique local projections onto \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is locally prox-regular when one positive radius gives a uniform quadratic support inequality for all nearby unit proximal normals.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Prox-Regularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited Chapter 6 opening page is not a specific prox-regularity definition; the book inventory places prox-regularity in Chapter 13, Section F, page 609. A supporting definition and locator are required for the exact inequality and projection equivalence.

children.title: Uniform Prox-Regularity
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood-uniform projection and proximal-normal regularity.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is nonempty and closed in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform \(r\)-prox-regularity is equivalent to the global quadratic support inequality for all unit proximal normals.

notation.meaning: Proximal normal cone to C at x.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global uniform-radius form; neighborhood-uniform variants follow by restricting the quantified points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(C\) is uniformly \(r\)-prox-regular if
\[
\langle v,z-x\rangle\leq\frac{1}{2r}\|z-x\|^2
\]
for every \(x,z\in C\) and every \(v\in N_C^P(x)\) with \(\|v\|=1\). Equivalently, for every \(x\in C\), every such \(v\), and every \(t\in(0,r)\), the metric projection of \(x+tv\) onto \(C\) is uniquely \(x\). The same radius must work at every base point and normal direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform prox-regularity uses one radius for the quadratic normal inequality, or equivalently for unique projection along every short proximal-normal displacement.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Prox-Regularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The global quadratic condition is plausible, but the cited page does not specifically support uniform prox-regularity or its stated projection equivalence.

children.title: Positive-Reach Geometry
children.top_down_role: Reach and tubular-neighborhood regimes for stable projection.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{reach}(C)>0\) exactly when projection onto \(C\) is single-valued throughout some open tubular neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Federer reach expressed through uniqueness of nearest points in a tubular neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The reach of \(C\) is
\[
\operatorname{reach}(C):=\sup\{r\geq0: P_C(y)\text{ is a singleton whenever }d_C(y)<r\}.
\]
Thus \(C\) has positive reach if and only if there exists \(r>0\) for which every point in the open tube \(\{y:d_C(y)<r\}\) has a unique nearest point in \(C\). For a closed Euclidean set, this is the global tubular-neighborhood form of uniform prox-regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reach is the largest tubular radius within which every ambient point has a unique nearest point on the set. Positive reach is global uniform prox-regularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Reach Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reach definition is standard, but the supplied Chapter 6 page does not specifically support it or the asserted equivalence with global uniform prox-regularity.

children.title: Prox-Regularity Stability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Behavior of prox-regular geometry under intersections, transformations, and singular limits.

children.title: Prox-Regularity under Smooth Transformations
children.top_down_role: Persistence of prox-regular geometry through regular smooth coordinate changes.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is locally prox-regular at \(\bar x\).
\(F:X\to Y\) is a \(C^{1,1}\) diffeomorphism between neighborhoods of \(\bar x\) and \(F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(C)\) is locally prox-regular at \(F(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Inverse transpose of the derivative of F.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance under locally bi-Lipschitz smooth coordinate changes with Lipschitz derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated hypotheses, the image \(F(C)\) is locally prox-regular at \(F(\bar x)\). More precisely, after shrinking the neighborhoods, proximal-normal estimates for \(C\), the local bounds on \(DF\) and \(DF^{-1}\), and the Lipschitz modulus of \(DF\) yield a positive prox-regularity radius for \(F(C)\). Normal directions transform locally according to the inverse-transpose rule \(w=DF(x)^{-T}v\), followed by normalization. Mere differentiability without local invertibility and Lipschitz control of the derivative does not ensure this conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally prox-regular set remains locally prox-regular under a local C1,1 diffeomorphism; the new radius depends on derivative, inverse, and curvature bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regularity under Smooth Transformations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the stability leaf, but the precise C1,1 hypotheses, transformed-normal rule, and preservation conclusion require a specific authoritative source.

children.title: Prox-Regularity under Regular Intersections
children.top_down_role: Persistence of prox-regular geometry for suitably compatible set intersections.

assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subset X\) are locally prox-regular at \(\bar x\in\bigcap_i C_i\).
The normal qualification \(\sum_{i=1}^m v_i=0\), \(v_i\in N_{C_i}(\bar x)\), implies \(v_i=0\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\) is locally prox-regular at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: Limiting normal cone to the ith set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite intersections under a strong normal transversality qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C:=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\). If the stated normal qualification holds and persists after restricting to a sufficiently small neighborhood of \(\bar x\), then \(C\) is locally prox-regular at \(\bar x\). In particular, nearby normals to the intersection admit controlled decompositions into normals to the component sets, and their individual quadratic support inequalities combine into one quadratic support inequality for \(C\). The persistence requirement is automatic under standard finite-dimensional outer-semicontinuity and quantitative transversality formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite intersection of locally prox-regular sets is locally prox-regular when their nearby normal cones satisfy a quantitative transversality condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regularity under Regular Intersections

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The assumptions state only a pointwise normal qualification, while the statement additionally requires neighborhood persistence. A source is needed to determine whether the pointwise condition suffices or must be replaced by quantitative nearby transversality.

children.title: Prox-Regularity Failure in Singular Limits
children.top_down_role: Loss of prox-regular structure under geometrically singular limiting processes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_k\to C\) locally while every \(C_k\) is locally prox-regular and \(C\) is not prox-regular at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth curves converging to a zero-reach V-shaped limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Each \(C_k\) is a smooth embedded curve and hence is locally prox-regular at every point. The sets \(C_k\) converge locally in Hausdorff distance to \(C\), but their curvature near \((0,k^{-1/2})\) is unbounded as \(k\to\infty\), so no common positive prox-regularity radius survives. For every \(t>0\), the point \((0,t)\) has two nearest points on \(C\), namely \((t/2,t/2)\) and \((-t/2,t/2)\). Therefore \(C\) has zero local reach and is not prox-regular at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth rounded V-curves are locally prox-regular but converge to a V-shaped curve having two arbitrarily close nearest-point projections, so prox-regularity is lost.
knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regularity Failure in Singular Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit rounded-V construction is mathematically coherent and its counterexample kind fits the failure leaf, but no cited source supports this nontrivial example.

children.title: Prox-Regularity Failure at Nontransversal Intersections
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of prox-regular geometry where intersecting sets meet degenerately.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(A\) and \(B\) are locally prox-regular, \(A\cap B\) is not prox-regular at the origin.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangential smooth surfaces whose intersection is a non-prox-regular crossing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Both \(A\) and \(B\) are smooth embedded surfaces and therefore locally prox-regular. At the origin their normal spaces coincide, so the intersection transversality qualification fails. Their intersection is
\[
A\cap B=\{(x,y,0):xy=0\},
\]
the union of the two coordinate axes in the plane \(z=0\). For every \(t>0\), the point \((t,t,0)\) has the two distinct nearest points \((t,0,0)\) and \((0,t,0)\) in \(A\cap B\). Hence projection is multivalued arbitrarily close to the origin, and the intersection is not prox-regular there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two smooth prox-regular surfaces can meet tangentially in crossed axes. Nearby points then have two projections, so their intersection is not prox-regular.
knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regularity Failure at Nontransversal Intersections

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tangential-surface construction is mathematically coherent and fits the failure leaf, but the nontrivial counterexample has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Set-System Regularity
children.top_down_role: Geometric regularity of collections of intersecting sets.

children.title: Transversality
children.top_down_role: Robust separation of normal systems at intersections.

knowledge_statements.title: Transversality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional normal-cone qualification for a finite family of closed sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family \(\{A_i\}_{i=1}^m\) is transversal at \(\bar x\) in the normal-cone sense if the only balanced collection of limiting normals is the zero collection: whenever \(v_i\in N_{A_i}(\bar x)\) for every \(i\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^m v_i=0\), one has \(v_i=0\) for all \(i\). Equivalently, no nonzero normals to the individual sets can cancel at the intersection point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transversality excludes cancellation among nonzero limiting normals to the sets at their common point.
assumptions_latex: \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\subset X\) are closed and \(\bar x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m A_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left[v_i\in N_{A_i}(\bar x)\ \text{for all }i\ \text{and}\ \sum_{i=1}^m v_i=0\right]\Longrightarrow v_1=\cdots=v_m=0\).

notation.meaning: Limiting normal cone to the set A at x.

children.title: Subtransversality
children.top_down_role: Error-bound-oriented regularity of set intersections.

assumptions_latex: \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\subset X\) are closed near \(\bar x\in A:=\bigcap_{i=1}^m A_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(x,A)\leq \kappa\max_{1\leq i\leq m}d(x,A_i)\) for every \(x\in B_\delta(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Distance from x to a set S.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local metric error-bound formulation for a finite set family.

source_refs.locator: 5.4.1 Linear Subextremality of Set Systems p. 110
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The family \(\{A_i\}_{i=1}^m\) is subtransversal at \(\bar x\) if there exist constants \(\kappa>0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
d\!\left(x,\bigcap_{i=1}^m A_i\right)\leq \kappa\max_{1\leq i\leq m}d(x,A_i)
\]
for every \(x\in B_\delta(\bar x)\). Thus the largest individual feasibility residual locally controls distance to the common intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtransversality is a local error bound controlling distance to the intersection by the largest individual set residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Subtransversality

source_witnesses.locator: 5.4.1 Linear Subextremality of Set Systems p. 110
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

children.title: Linear Regularity of Set Families
children.top_down_role: Quantitative regularity of finite and structured set collections.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Regularity of Set Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric linear regularity on a prescribed region; bounded and local variants follow by choosing the region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite family \(\{A_i\}_{i=1}^m\) is linearly regular on \(S\subset X\) if there exists \(\kappa>0\) such that
\[
d\!\left(x,A\right)\leq \kappa\max_{1\leq i\leq m}d(x,A_i)\qquad\text{for all }x\in S,
\]
where \(A=\bigcap_{i=1}^m A_i\). It is boundedly linearly regular when such a constant exists separately on every bounded \(S\), and locally linearly regular at \(\bar x\in A\) when it holds on some neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear regularity quantitatively bounds distance to a common intersection by the largest distance to an individual set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(x,A)\leq\kappa\max_i d(x,A_i)\) on the specified region \(S\).

notation.meaning: Region on which regularity is asserted.
Distance from x to a set C.

source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II
source_refs.locator: 5.4.1 Linear Subextremality of Set Systems p. 110

source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II
source_witnesses.locator: 5.4.1 Linear Subextremality of Set Systems p. 110

children.title: Intrinsic Transversality
children.top_down_role: Intersection regularity expressed through relative normal geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(A,B\) are closed subsets of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniformly near \(\bar x\), oppositely oriented relative proximal normals cannot have normalized sum tending to zero.

notation.meaning: Proximal normal cone to C at c.
Open ball centered at the reference point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential relative-proximal-normal formulation for two closed sets in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The pair \(\{A,B\}\) is intrinsically transversal at \(\bar x\) if there exist \(\alpha>0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that, whenever \(a\in(A\setminus B)\cap B_\delta(\bar x)\), \(b\in(B\setminus A)\cap B_\delta(\bar x)\), and nonzero \(u\in N_A^P(a)\), \(v\in N_B^P(b)\) are relative normals directed approximately toward the other set, one has
\[
\left\|\frac{u}{\|u\|}+\frac{v}{\|v\|}\right\|\geq\alpha.
\]
Thus no admissible sequence of relative unit normals can become exactly opposite while its base points approach \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intrinsic transversality uniformly prevents relative proximal normals of two sets from becoming opposite near their intersection.
knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic Transversality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The qualitative idea fits intrinsic transversality, but “directed approximately toward the other set” is not a quantified condition. Definitions vary among proximal, restricted-normal, and sequential formulations, so an authoritative locator is required before the mathematical version can be fixed.

children.title: Geometric Irregularity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Canonical local phenomena that destabilize first-order geometric models.

children.title: Singular Local Geometry Family
children.top_down_role: Rapidly varying or singular local geometry with unstable first-order models.

children.title: Oscillatory Local Geometry
children.top_down_role: Rapid local variation that destabilizes first-order geometric descriptions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tangent lines at smooth points approaching \((0,0)\) have no unique limiting orientation.

notation.meaning: Bouligand tangent cone to C at z.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct differentiation of the displayed curve
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A planar oscillatory graph exhibiting unstable local tangent orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x>0\), the set \(C\) is locally a smooth curve with tangent direction
\[
\left(1,\sin(1/x)-\frac{\cos(1/x)}{x}\right).
\]
As \(x\downarrow0\), the second component is unbounded along sequences with \(\cos(1/x)\neq0\), while along sequences satisfying \(\cos(1/x)=0\) it equals \(\pm1\). Hence the tangent lines \(T_C((x,x\sin(1/x)))\) do not approach a unique line at the origin, despite all base points converging to \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oscillating graph has tangent lines with incompatible limiting orientations at the origin.
knowledge_statements.title: Oscillatory Local Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The oscillatory-curve phenomenon fits the leaf, but no cited source supports it, the statement includes a derivation, and the assertion about sequences with nonzero cosine needs more precise quantification.

children.title: Cuspidal Local Geometry
children.top_down_role: Singular pointed geometry near cusp-like loci.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \(\{A,B\}\) is not subtransversal at \((0,0)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: displayed asymptotic estimates directly refute the error bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two tangent semicubical cusp branches violating a linear intersection error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sets meet only at \(\bar x=(0,0)\). For \(z_t=(t^2,t^3)\in A\) with \(t>0\),
\[
d(z_t,A\cap B)=\|z_t\|\sim t^2,
\qquad d(z_t,B)\leq\|(t^2,t^3)-(t^2,-t^3)\|=2t^3.
\]
Consequently \(d(z_t,A\cap B)/\max\{d(z_t,A),d(z_t,B)\}\to\infty\). No local constant \(\kappa\) can satisfy the subtransversality error bound, showing how cuspidal tangency destroys linear regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two cusp branches approach each other cubically while approaching their intersection quadratically, so the linear error bound fails.
knowledge_statements.title: Cuspidal Local Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cusp example and failure of the local linear error bound are plausible and fit the leaf, but the record supplies an argument instead of a cited statement and has no inspectable source locator.

children.title: Tangent Instability
children.top_down_role: Variation or nonuniqueness of tangent behavior near irregular points.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^2\) is the union of rays with angles \(0,1,1/2,1/3,\ldots\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tangent-cone mapping \(x\mapsto T_C(x)\) is not inner semicontinuous at the origin.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: tangent cones follow directly from the ray-union geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A closed union of rays whose tangent-cone mapping loses directions immediately away from the vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C:=R_0\cup\bigcup_{n\geq1}R_{1/n}.
\]
At the origin, \(T_C(0)=C\), so in particular the direction \((\cos1,\sin1)\) belongs to \(T_C(0)\). For any sequence \(x_k\in R_0\setminus\{0\}\) with \(x_k\to0\), a sufficiently small neighborhood of \(x_k\) meets only \(R_0\), and therefore \(T_C(x_k)=\mathbb R(1,0)\). No sequence of directions from \(T_C(x_k)\) can converge to \((\cos1,\sin1)\), proving inner semicontinuity fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a union-of-rays vertex the tangent cone contains many directions, but nearby tangent cones may contain only one.
knowledge_statements.title: Tangent Instability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed counterexample is incorrect. Every neighborhood of a nonzero point on the limiting ray R_0 meets rays R_{1/n}; hence the claim that a sufficiently small neighborhood meets only R_0, and the resulting computation of the nearby tangent cone, are false.

children.title: Projection Instability
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity or multiplicity of nearby projection behavior.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The metric projector \(P_C\) is multivalued at points arbitrarily close to the cusp.

notation.meaning: Set of nearest points in C to z.
Positive point on the cusp axis.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: symmetry and one-variable minimization establish the displayed nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nearest-point nonuniqueness arbitrarily close to a semicubical cusp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(s>0\), minimizing the squared distance from \(z_s=(s,0)\) to \(C\) reduces, with \(u=t^2\geq0\), to minimizing
\[
\phi_s(u)=(u-s)^2+u^3.
\]
Its positive minimizer \(u_s\) satisfies \(3u_s^2+2u_s-2s=0\). Both parameters \(t=\sqrt{u_s}\) and \(t=-\sqrt{u_s}\) therefore give distinct nearest points \((u_s,\pm u_s^{3/2})\). Since \(z_s\to(0,0)\), the projector is not single-valued on any neighborhood of the cusp.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every neighborhood of a semicubical cusp contains points having two symmetric nearest points on the curve.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Instability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection nonuniqueness claim is mathematically plausible and fits projection instability, but no source with an inspectable locator is cited and the statement contains the one-variable minimization argument.

children.title: Closure-Attainment Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Closure and attainment failures in local direction and projection constructions.

children.title: Nonclosed Local Direction Models
children.top_down_role: Local direction systems whose natural geometric realizations require closure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The radial direction cone \(R_C(\bar z)\) is not closed, while \(T_C(\bar z)=\overline{R_C(\bar z)}\).

notation.meaning: Radial cone of C at z.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: both cones are computed directly from the displayed epigraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex epigraph with a nonclosed cone of exactly realizable radial directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A direct calculation gives
\[
R_C(\bar z)=\{(a,b):b>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\},
\qquad T_C(\bar z)=\{(a,b):b\geq0\}.
\]
Indeed, every direction with positive second component can be scaled to reach the epigraph, whereas a nonzero horizontal direction cannot. Nevertheless horizontal directions arise as limits of directions with positive second component. Thus the exact radial model is nonclosed even though \(C\) itself is closed and convex, and tangent formation fills the closure gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed parabolic epigraph has a nonclosed radial cone; its tangent cone adds the missing horizontal directions by closure.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Local Direction Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The radial- and tangent-cone calculations fit the nonclosed-direction-model leaf, but they are unsupported by a cited source and are presented with derivational text.

children.title: Nonattained Local Projection Models
children.top_down_role: Local projection or nearest-point descriptions lacking attained representatives.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C(0)=\varnothing\), although \(C\) is closed and \(d(0,C)=1\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pairwise separation proves closedness and the displayed norms prove nonattainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed nonconvex subset of an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space with an unattained nearest-point distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Distinct elements of \(C\) are uniformly separated because
\[
\|(1+1/n)e_n-(1+1/m)e_m\|^2=(1+1/n)^2+(1+1/m)^2
\]
for \(m\neq n\); hence \(C\) is closed. However,
\[
d(0,C)=\inf_{n\geq1}(1+1/n)=1,
\]
and no element of \(C\) has norm \(1\). Therefore the nearest-point set \(P_C(0)\) is empty. Closedness alone does not guarantee projection attainment for nonconvex sets in infinite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed discrete subset of Hilbert space can approach an unattained minimum distance, leaving the metric projection empty.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonattained Local Projection Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The infinite-dimensional nonattainment example is correct in form and fits the leaf, but it has no inspectable citation and includes the closedness and nonattainment argument.

children.title: Closure-Gap Consequences
children.top_down_role: Geometric distinctions created by passing from raw local models to their closures.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The direction \((1,0)\) is tangent at \(\bar z\) but is not an exactly feasible radial direction.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the explicit sequence demonstrates the closure gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequences of replacing an exact direction model by its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the parabolic epigraph,
\[
(1,0)\in T_C(\bar z)\setminus R_C(\bar z).
\]
The tangent membership is witnessed by \(t_k\downarrow0\), \(c_k=(t_k,t_k^2)\in C\), and \(c_k/t_k=(1,t_k)\to(1,0)\). Yet no \(t>0\) satisfies \(\bar z+t(1,0)\in C\). Consequently a closed tangent model may certify a limiting first-order direction that has no exactly feasible ray, so conclusions requiring exact radial realization cannot be transferred across the closure operation without an additional derivability assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing a radial model can add tangent directions that are only asymptotically, never exactly, feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Gap Consequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closure-gap phenomenon and failure-boundary classification fit the target, but the claim has no cited source and its witness construction is proof text.

children.title: Attainment-Loss Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes separating stable realization from merely asymptotic local behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(C\subset H\) is nonempty.
For some \(x\in H\) and \(r>d(x,C)\), the set \(C\cap\overline B_r(x)\) is compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The distance \(d(x,C)\) is attained; loss of compactness permits failure even when \(C\) is closed.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: compactness gives attainment of the continuous distance function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness boundary separating guaranteed nearest-point attainment from infinite-dimensional failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the compactness assumption, the continuous function \(c\mapsto\|x-c\|\) attains its minimum on \(C\cap\overline B_r(x)\), and every sufficiently accurate minimizing point lies in that set; hence \(P_C(x)\neq\varnothing\). This guarantee can fail when bounded minimizing sequences lack convergent subsequences. In \(\ell^2\), the closed set \(C=\{(1+1/n)e_n:n\geq1\}\) satisfies \(d(0,C)=1\) but \(P_C(0)=\varnothing\), locating the boundary at loss of the relevant compactness or an alternative proximinality condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local compactness guarantees distance attainment; without it, a closed infinite-dimensional set may still have no nearest point.
knowledge_statements.title: Attainment-Loss Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compactness attainment boundary and the contrasting Hilbert-space example are mathematically plausible and appropriately classified, but neither is supported by an inspectable citation and the statement includes explanatory proof text.

children.title: Infinite-Dimensional Compactness Failures
children.top_down_role: Loss of sequential compactness and exact limiting calculus in Banach spaces.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bounded sequence \((e_n)\) converges weakly to \(0\) but has no norm-convergent subsequence; thus bounded subsets of \(H\) need not be sequentially compact in the norm topology.

notation.meaning: An orthonormal sequence in the Hilbert space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical Hilbert-space obstruction motivating additional compactness assumptions in infinite-dimensional limiting-normal calculus.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.4 Sequential Normal Compactness of Sets p. 27
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((e_n)\) be an orthonormal sequence in \(H\). Then \(\lVert e_n\rVert=1\) for every \(n\), \(\lVert e_n-e_m\rVert=\sqrt{2}\) for distinct \(n,m\), and \(e_n\rightharpoonup0\). Consequently, \((e_n)\) is bounded and weakly convergent but has no norm-convergent subsequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthonormal sequence in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space converges weakly to zero but has no norm-convergent subsequence, demonstrating failure of norm sequential compactness for bounded sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Dimensional Compactness Failures

notation.meaning: Contingent tangent cone to the feasible set

For every feasible tangent direction \(d\in T_C( ar x)\), differentiability and local minimality give \(\langle

children.title: Multiplier Certificates
children.top_down_role: Geometric organization of constraint certificates expressed through multipliers.

assumptions_latex: \(p,q\in\mathbb{N}\), and \(f,g_i,h_j:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\) for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\) and \(j\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\).
The feasible set is \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g_i(x)\le0\text{ for all }i,\ h_j(x)=0\text{ for all }j\}\), and \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
There exist \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^p\) and \(\mu\in\mathbb{R}^q\) such that \(
abla f( ar x)+\sum_{i=1}^p\lambda_i
abla g_i( ar x)+\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_j
abla h_j( ar x)=0\) and \(\lambda_i g_i( ar x)=0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\).

abla h_j( ar x)=0,\qquad \lambda_i g_i( ar x)=0\quad	ext{for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}.\] These relations, together with primal feasibility, constitute the KKT multiplier certificate at \( ar x\).

children.title: Multiplier–Normal Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural linkage between multiplier representations and normal-cone membership.

assumptions_latex: \(p,q\in\mathbb{N}\), and \(g_i,h_j:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\) for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\) and \(j\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\).

notation.meaning: Limiting normal cone to the feasible set

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under MFCQ, every feasible-set normal is a nonnegative linear combination of active inequality gradients plus a linear combination of equality gradients.

children.title: Certificate Breakdown under Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Loss of faithful multiplier or normal-certificate interpretation in degenerate regimes.

assumptions_latex: The problem is to minimize \(f(x)\) subject to \(g(x)\le0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x=0\) is a constrained minimizer, but no KKT multiplier exists because \(1+\lambda\,0\ne0\) for every \(\lambda\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary smooth example where degeneracy destroys the normalized KKT certificate despite local optimality.

source_refs.locator: 5.1.3 Necessary Conditions under Functional Constraints p. 22
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The constraint \(x^2\le0\) has the singleton feasible set \(C=\{0\}\), so \(\bar x=0\) is a local and global minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\). Yet \(\nabla f(0)=1\) and \(\nabla g(0)=0\). KKT stationarity would require \(1+\lambda\,0=0\) for some \(\lambda\ge0\), which is impossible. The normal cone is nevertheless \(N_C(0)=\mathbb{R}\), showing that the failed constraint gradient cannot represent the genuine geometric normals. Thus local optimality survives while the normalized multiplier certificate breaks down.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimizing x subject to x²≤0, zero is the only feasible point and hence optimal, but the vanishing constraint gradient makes KKT stationarity impossible.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Breakdown under Degeneracy

assumptions_latex: \(p,q\in\mathbb{N}\), and \(f,g_i,h_j:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) are continuously differentiable near a feasible local minimizer \(\bar x\), for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\) and \(j\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\).
A Fritz John multiplier tuple \((\alpha,\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}_+\times\mathbb{R}_+^p\times\mathbb{R}^q\) is nonzero and satisfies stationarity and complementary slackness at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Fritz John certificate is abnormal if and only if \(\alpha=0\).

A nonzero Fritz John tuple \((\alpha,\lambda,mu)\in\mathbb{R}_+	imes\mathbb{R}_+^p	imes\mathbb{R}^q\) satisfies \[\alpha
abla f( ar x)+\sum_{i=1}^p\lambda_i
abla g_i( ar x)+\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_j

children.title: Degenerate Multiplier Geometry
children.top_down_role: Multiplier behavior shaped by deficient or redundant local constraint geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb{R}^q\to\mathbb{R}^n\) maps active multiplier coordinates to their linear combination of active constraint gradients.
A multiplier \(y\) represents a fixed normal vector \(v\) through \(Ay=v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonzero \(z\in\ker A\) preserving multiplier sign restrictions generates equivalent certificates \(y+t z\) and therefore degeneracy or nonuniqueness.

notation.meaning: Multiplier coordinates and a null direction
Normal vector represented by the multipliers

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear geometry of degeneracy in a smooth active-constraint multiplier representation.

source_refs.locator: 5.1.3 Necessary Conditions under Functional Constraints p. 22

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write the active-gradient representation as \(Ay=v\), with inequality coordinates of \(y\) constrained to be nonnegative and equality coordinates unrestricted. If \(z\in\ker A\), then \(A(y+t z)=v\) for every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\). Hence every value of \(t\) for which the inequality coordinates of \(y+t z\) remain nonnegative produces the same normal certificate. A nontrivial kernel records linear dependence among active gradients; if it contains a feasible multiplier direction, the representation is locally nonunique. When \(v=0\), a nonzero sign-compatible kernel vector is an abnormal constraint-only certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear dependence among active gradients creates kernel directions in multiplier space; sign-compatible kernel directions preserve the represented normal and generate degenerate or nonunique certificates.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Multiplier Geometry

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: MFCQ fails at \(\bar x\) if and only if either \(\{\nabla h_j(\bar x)\}_{j=1}^q\) is linearly dependent or no \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies all equality-tangency and strict active-inequality decrease conditions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
MFCQ fails at \( ar x\) if and only if at least one of the following holds: \(\{
abla h_j( ar x)\}_{j=1}^q\) is linearly dependent; or there is no \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[\langle
abla h_j( ar x),dangle=0\quad	ext{for every }j\in\{1,\ldots,q\},\qquad \langle
abla g_i( ar x),dangle<0\quad	ext{for every }i\in I( ar x).\]

children.title: Nonunique Certificate Geometry
children.top_down_role: Local geometric sources of multiple or weakly identifiable multiplier certificates.

assumptions_latex: A fixed feasible point \(\bar x\) and a fixed stationarity vector determine a linear multiplier system.
Inequality multipliers are constrained to be nonnegative and inactive ones vanish.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certificate set is a convex polyhedron and is nonunique exactly when it contains two distinct multiplier vectors.

notation.meaning: Linear stationarity map formed from active gradients

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex geometry of multipliers for one fixed smooth KKT stationarity system.

source_refs.locator: 5.1.3 Necessary Conditions under Functional Constraints p. 22
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The multiplier certificate set has the form
\[
\Lambda=\{y\in K:Ay=b\},
\]
where the nonnegative coordinates correspond to active inequalities and the free coordinates to equalities. Hence \(\Lambda\) is the intersection of an affine space with a polyhedral cone and is therefore convex and polyhedral. If \(y^1,y^2\in\Lambda\) are distinct, then every \((1-t)y^1+t y^2\) with \(t\in[0,1]\) is another certificate. Equivalently, nonuniqueness occurs when some nonzero \(z\in\ker A\) connects two sign-admissible multiplier vectors; uniqueness requires that no such admissible kernel displacement exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed smooth stationarity system, admissible multipliers form a convex polyhedron; any sign-compatible null direction produces a continuum of equivalent certificates.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Certificate Geometry

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle F(\bar x),x-\bar x\rangle\ge0\) for all \(x\in C\) if and only if \(0\in F(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Convex-analytic normal cone to the feasible set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex variational inequality as a normal-cone generalized equation.

source_refs.locator: IV.9 A Variational Inequality with Mixed Boundary Conditions p. 139
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
By definition of the convex normal cone,
\[
-F(\bar x)\in N_C(\bar x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\langle-F(\bar x),x-\bar x\rangle\le0\quad\text{for every }x\in C.
\]
Therefore the variational inequality \(\langle F(\bar x),x-\bar x\rangle\ge0\) for all \(x\in C\) is equivalent to the generalized equation \(0\in F(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x)\). Its local feasible-direction consequence is \(\langle F(\bar x),d\rangle\ge0\) for every \(d\in T_C(\bar x)\); convexity makes this tangent geometry equivalent to the global inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex variational inequality is exactly the normal-cone inclusion that the negative field value is normal to the feasible set at the solution.

children.title: Complementarity Geometry
children.top_down_role: Active-set and normal geometry associated with complementarity systems.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le a\perp b\ge0\) means \((a,b)\in\bigcup_{I\subset\{1,\ldots,m\}}F_I\), a union of complementary coordinate faces.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative orthant and its dual cone
Complementary coordinate face indexed by a subset

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthant complementarity represented as a nonconvex union of complementary coordinate faces.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Constrained Optimization and Equilibria p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The complementarity set is
\[
\mathcal C=\{(a,b)\in K\times K^*: \langle a,b\rangle=0\}
=\{(a,b):a_i\ge0,\ b_i\ge0,\ a_i b_i=0\ \text{for every }i\}.
\]
For each \(I\subset\{1,\ldots,m\}\), define
\[
F_I=\{(a,b):a_I=0,\ b_{I^c}=0,\ a_{I^c}\ge0,\ b_I\ge0\}.
\]
Then \(\mathcal C=\bigcup_I F_I\). Thus complementarity geometry is a finite union of convex polyhedral faces, generally nonconvex at points where some pair satisfies \(a_i=b_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthant complementarity is a finite union of coordinate faces, becoming geometrically nonconvex where both members of a complementary pair vanish.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity Geometry

children.title: Equilibrium Geometry
children.top_down_role: Local variational geometry associated with equilibrium conditions.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
The dual cone is defined by \(C^*=\{z:\langle z,y\rangle\ge 0\ \forall y\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F)\iff x\in C,\ F(x)\in C^*,\ \langle x,F(x)\rangle=0\).

notation.meaning: solution set of the variational inequality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic variational inequalities represented as complementarity equilibria.

source_refs.locator: 5.2.2 Variational Systems as Equilibrium Constraints p. 51
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in C\), define equilibrium by the variational inequality \(\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(y\in C\). Because \(C\) is a cone, this condition is equivalent to the conic complementarity system \[x\in C,\qquad F(x)\in C^*,\qquad \langle x,F(x)\rangle=0.\] Consequently, the equilibrium solution set satisfies \[\operatorname{SOL}(C,F)=\{x\in C:F(x)\in C^*,\ \langle x,F(x)\rangle=0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic variational-inequality equilibrium is exactly a complementary pair formed by the state and its residual.

children.title: Critical-Cone Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Critical-direction structures connecting local constraints to complementarity or equilibrium behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(x\in C\) and \(v\in N_C(x)\), where \(N_C(x)=\{w\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle w,y-x\rangle\le 0\ \forall y\in C\}\).
\(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is single-valued for the variational-inequality specialization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_C(x,v)=T_C(x)\cap v^\perp\); if \(-F(x)\in N_C(x)\), then \(K_C(x,-F(x))=T_C(x)\cap F(x)^\perp\).

notation.meaning: Bouligand tangent cone to C at x
convex normal cone to C at x
critical cone associated with x and v

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The critical cone of \(C\) at \(x\) relative to the normal \(v\) is \[K_C(x,v):=T_C(x)\cap v^\perp=\{d\in T_C(x):\langle v,d\rangle=0\}.\] If \(x\) solves the variational inequality generated by \(F\), equivalently \(-F(x)\in N_C(x)\), then its equilibrium critical cone is \[K_C(x,-F(x))=T_C(x)\cap F(x)^\perp.\] Thus it consists precisely of the feasible first-order directions orthogonal to the equilibrium normal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The critical cone consists of feasible tangent directions orthogonal to the specified normal; at a variational-inequality solution, that normal is the negative residual.

children.title: Active-Face Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Face-based organization of local complementarity and equilibrium regimes.

assumptions_latex: For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(b_i\in\mathbb{R}\), and suppose \(C=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^Tz\le b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) is nonempty.
Define \(I(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:a_i^Tx=b_i\}\), and fix multipliers \(\lambda_i\ge 0\) for \(i\in I(x)\) such that \(-F(x)=\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i a_i\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the fixed multiplier vector, the tangent cone is \[T_C(x)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^Td\le 0\ \text{for every }i\in I(x)\}.\] Because \(-F(x)=\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i a_i\), its orthogonality condition on this tangent cone is equivalent to equality for every index in \(I_+(x)\). Therefore, \[K_C(x,-F(x))=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^Td\le 0\ \forall i\in I(x),\quad a_i^Td=0\ \forall i\in I_+(x)\}.\] This critical cone is the face of \(T_C(x)\) exposed by the equilibrium normal \(-F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed multiplier representation of the equilibrium normal, the positively weighted active constraints identify the tangent-cone face equal to the equilibrium critical cone.
